Table 5: Comparison with concurrent world-action models

synopsis: GlanceWAM uses a shared video diffusion transformer to imagine a roughly three-second visual destination, then conditions an inverse-dynamics action head on that destination in latent space. It reports 72.2% simulated manipulation success on RoboCasa and 99.0% on LIBERO. The central evidence supports useful lookahead conditioning and fast action decoding with a cached lookahead. However, the asynchronous success experiment refreshes every action chunk, whereas the proposed sparse schedule refreshes every few seconds; these are materially different deployment settings. [e02, e05, e07, e09, e10, e14, e17]

problem.text: The authors argue that generating future video synchronously for every action chunk makes control slow and confines prediction to short, nearly static transitions. Removing inference-time prediction saves computation but can remove useful visual guidance. Their objective is to retain a distant visual target while allowing action decoding to proceed independently of video sampling.

contributions.text: A shared video DiT supports both latent future generation and observation/lookahead feature extraction for an action head, with generation assigned to a slower asynchronous process.
Two separate causal-VAE passes and a three-role attention mask prevent the clean teacher-forced lookahead from leaking into the future-prediction stream.

Randomized lookahead offsets train the policy to consume an aging destination. Internal interventions establish dependence on this conditioning channel, while sampler sweeps suggest that substantially more generation steps are unnecessary in the tested setting.

inputs: Observation history o≤t containing RGB camera views, plus language instruction c. [e02, e08]
Training: demonstration action chunks, a future frame at t+H_f, and a separate clean lookahead frame at t+u. [e03, e05]
Action inference: current observation features, a generated lookahead latent and its temporal offset Δ. [e07]
outputs: A generated latent visual destination approximately H_f seconds ahead. [e07]
A continuous action chunk for environment execution, decoded from observation and lookahead features. [e05, e07]

steps.name: Construct distinct prediction and guidance streams
steps.detail: Training supplies clean observations, a noised future target at the full foresight horizon, and a clean intermediate lookahead. One causal-VAE pass encodes observations with the future target; another encodes observations with the lookahead. This prevents temporal compression from mixing the full-horizon target into the policy's guidance latent.

steps.name: Apply directional attention isolation
steps.detail: Observation queries read only observations. Future queries read observations and future tokens. Lookahead queries read observations and lookahead tokens. Thus neither observation nor future-prediction representations can directly read the clean lookahead through transformer attention.

steps.name: Learn prediction and inverse dynamics
steps.detail: The shared backbone predicts future-latent flow velocity. A separate flow-matching action head predicts action velocity conditioned on observation/lookahead representations, language and offset. The final model extracts features from DiT layers {5,12,19,26}.

steps.name: Generate and retain a latent destination
steps.detail: At deployment, the video sampler predicts a lookahead from observation and language context without conditioning on a candidate action sequence. The resulting latent becomes the clean lookahead input for policy passes; it is not decoded into RGB for control.

steps.name: Decode actions against the held destination
steps.detail: Each action pass combines updated observation features with the held lookahead and its remaining offset. A clean backbone forward supplies features to the action head. The measured LIBERO implementation still performs four action-flow steps; the single-pass description applies to the backbone, not the entire action sampler.

training.text: The video DiT and action head are optimized jointly with equal-weight video and action flow losses. The policy receives teacher-forced demonstration lookaheads, sampled with u uniformly distributed over (0,H_f], a sinusoidal embedding of Δ=u, and lookahead dropout of 0.1.

Training initializes from SkyReels-V2-DF-1.3B and uses demonstrations without online rollouts or auxiliary depth/contact labels. The reported schedules are 10,000 steps for RoboCasa and 15,000 for LIBERO, with EMA checkpoint evaluation.

inference.text: The main formulation uses H_f≈3 seconds and 16-action chunks at 20 Hz, lasting 0.8 seconds. A lookahead is intended to serve about four chunks. The latency evaluation instead uses LIBERO's eight-action chunks, so its timing configuration must remain distinct.

Appendix B's 478.6 ms measurement is an unoptimized ten-step refresh call that generates a lookahead and then acts on it, rather than an isolated generator measurement. The corresponding one-step refresh is approximately 145 ms. Background execution removes this work from the reported cached-lookahead path, but does not eliminate its compute cost.

equations.expression: L_video(θ_dit) = E_{τ,ε,z} ||v_θ(z_{t+H_f}^{(τ)}, τ | z_{≤t}, c) − (ε − z_{t+H_f})||²
equations.explanation: Equation (1) trains future-latent velocity prediction. τ is the future noise level, ε is sampled noise, and z denotes VAE latents. The clean policy lookahead is excluded from this predictor's conditioning.

equations.expression: L_action(θ_dit,ϕ_act) = E_{σ,ε_a,a} ||u_ϕ(a_t^{(σ)}, σ | [h_obs;h_la], c, Δ) − (ε_a − a_t)||²; L = L_video + L_action
equations.explanation: Equation (2) learns a velocity field over action chunks. σ is the action-flow timestep; h_obs and h_la are backbone features. This is the inverse-dynamics interface connecting a present observation and visual destination to actions.

equations.expression: u ~ U(0,H_f], Δ_train = u; Δ_infer = H_f − (t mod H_f)
equations.explanation: Training covers different remaining distances in time to the destination. The inference expression describes an ideal periodic hold cycle; it does not by itself account for a delayed proposal generated from an old observation.

results.setting: 24 tasks; 50 replay-filtered demonstrations per task; 1,200 evaluation episodes across five held-out layouts with unseen object instances.
results.comparison: Cosmos Policy: 67.1% with 50 demonstrations per task, a 5.1 percentage-point difference.
results.interpretation: Author-reported simulated task success. The baseline is imported from its publication under the adopted protocol; this is not a controlled retraining comparison or physical-robot result.

results.setting: Four suites of ten tasks each; 50 demonstrations and 50 evaluation episodes per task, totaling 2,000 evaluation episodes.
results.interpretation: The authors use this highly saturated simulated benchmark primarily for parity verification and latency evaluation. These small differences do not establish statistical superiority.

results.setting: RoboCasa internal comparisons sharing backbone, demonstration data and evaluation protocol; zeroing is applied to the single-layer checkpoint.
results.value: No lookahead: 64.4%; single-layer lookahead: 71.5%; multi-layer: 72.2%; single-layer checkpoint with lookahead zeroed: 61.6%.
results.comparison: Single-layer conditioning adds 7.1 percentage points; multi-layer extraction adds 0.7 points; zeroing removes 9.9 points from the single-layer checkpoint.
results.interpretation: The intervention demonstrates functional dependence on lookahead inputs. It does not independently establish that online forecasting, rather than the learned conditioning structure, explains the entire improvement.

results.setting: Single-layer RoboCasa checkpoint; paired re-evaluation with 1,200 episodes per sampler budget.
results.metric: Task success rate versus Euler steps
results.comparison: One step is 0.3 percentage points below ten steps; the full observed range is 1.9 points.
results.interpretation: Additional sampler steps do not consistently improve executed simulated-task success here. This is a control result, not a video-quality metric; uncertainty sufficient to establish equivalence is not supplied.

results.setting: RoboCasa horizon sweep described in Section 4.3.
results.value: 66.3% at H_f=1.4 seconds; 71.6% at 3.0 seconds; 71.1% at 3.8 seconds.
results.comparison: The three-second setting exceeds the 1.4-second setting by 5.3 percentage points.
results.interpretation: The reported sweep favors a more distant destination within the tested range. Values come from explicit prose, without inspecting Figure 6.

results.setting: Single-layer RoboCasa checkpoint; 1,200 paired episodes per arm. A new proposal is requested every 0.8-second chunk and adopted one chunk later.
results.metric: Task success rate and reported McNemar test
results.interpretation: This evaluates bounded one-chunk source staleness. Failure to detect a difference is not proof of equivalence, and this cadence does not validate refreshing only once every three seconds.

results.setting: Appendix D.1's separate naive-lag arms in the same paired RoboCasa sweep.
results.comparison: At 3.2 seconds, success is 12.8 percentage points below the zeroed reference.
results.interpretation: Expired guidance can actively harm control. These references belong to this sweep and should not be substituted for Table 3's different zeroing evaluation.

results.setting: LIBERO multi-layer checkpoint; batch size one; A100 SXM4 40 GB, bf16; eight-action chunks; 100 synchronized timed calls after 15 warmups; lookahead and text already cached.
results.metric: Wall-clock compute latency per action chunk
results.value: 47.95 ms, standard deviation 0.39 ms; headline value 48 ms.
results.comparison: Unoptimized GlanceWAM: 108.3 ms. Re-benchmarked compiled Fast-WAM: 91.5 ms, but with a 32-action chunk.
results.interpretation: This measures the optimized hold-phase path, not complete concurrent deployment latency. Different chunk lengths prevent interpreting the Fast-WAM ratio as an equivalent ratio in action throughput.

limitations.text: The deployment cadence is internally inconsistent. Section 3.4 proposes refreshes every H_f≈3 seconds, and Appendix B describes every 3–4 seconds; Appendix D.1 calls requesting every 0.8-second chunk the deployed configuration. Its small asynchronous success loss therefore does not establish the headline sparse-refresh configuration's success or amortized compute.

Offset randomization covers hold aging, but not generation from an observation already stale when the proposal is adopted. The authors explicitly identify this second condition as outside the training distribution. Teacher-forced real future frames also differ from generated deployment inputs.

The authors leave unresolved whether gains arise from additional test-time dynamics computation, from a training scaffold that separates destination from motion, or both. Zeroing establishes dependence but cannot distinguish these explanations.

The attention mask establishes forward information isolation at fixed weights. Because the action loss also updates the shared backbone, it does not establish that learned observation representations remain identical to a separately trained co-training baseline. The component table does not independently ablate the mask or two-pass encoding.

Evaluation concerns two simulation benchmarks. External baselines are taken from publications, training-step comparisons are explicitly not compute-matched, and comprehensive uncertainty across independent training runs is absent. Concurrent proposer/control resource contention is not established by the isolated latency measurements.

Several numerical descriptions disagree internally. Table 3 supports a 0.7-point multi-layer increment and a 7.8-point final gain over plain co-training, whereas prose elsewhere states 1.3 and 8.4. Appendix B's phase times sum to 48.9 ms rather than 47.95 ms, and its quoted 1–2 ms serving overhead does not fit straightforwardly inside a 48 ms total. The report retains the labeled table and aggregate measurements without resolving these discrepancies by assumption.

reproduction.text: Reproduction requires the SkyReels-V2-DF backbone, its causal VAE, benchmark demonstration splits, language conditioning and action interface. Appendix E specifies VAE temporal/spatial downsampling of 4/8, 16 latent channels and 2×2 latent patches. The supplied text does not specify action normalization, exact software versions or whether the VAE and text encoder are frozen.

The reported recipe uses four H200 GPUs, bf16 and total batch size 64; AdamW with β=(0.9,0.95), ε=10^-8, weight decay 10^-8 and gradient clipping 1.0. Backbone/head learning rates are 10^-5/10^-4, with 5,000 warmup steps and cosine decay to 5×10^-7. EMA decay is 0.999; action-head dropout is 0.2.

Matching latency requires GPU preprocessing, a backbone truncated to blocks 1–27, CUDA-graph compilation, cached instruction embeddings/lookahead/masks and a four-step action head. A meaningful verification should separately measure cached-lookahead latency, refresh compute and concurrent end-to-end latency under explicitly logged source/adoption timestamps.

A compact mechanism experiment would pair identical episode seeds across normal versus zeroed lookaheads and one-step versus ten-step generation, then vary refresh cadence separately from adoption delay. The authors link a code repository, but its contents were not inspected and no experiment was reproduced for this report.

reasoning.text: The core One Model × IDM quadrant is supported by architecture and inference evidence: a shared video DiT generates futures and supplies visual features, while its action head maps observations plus a future destination to actions. Joint losses do not imply joint future/action co-denoising at deployment. The efficiency tag is supported specifically for the cached-lookahead action path. The memory subcategory is supported only in the limited sense of retaining a future latent across chunks; persistent long-term memory is not demonstrated.

discussionQuestions: Does the success advantage persist when refresh frequency and source-observation age are varied independently, including the proposed once-per-H_f schedule? [e07, e17]
Can an equal-compute policy control distinguish useful online forecasting from the training scaffold created by future-conditioned inverse dynamics? [e16]
Can a timestamp-aware fallback detect expired lookaheads before they become worse than removing the conditioning channel? [e17]

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title block, author list and arXiv version line
evidence.detail: The title and ten authors match the catalog; the supplied paper identifies itself as arXiv:2608.23927v1, dated 25 August 2026.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 1–2, Section 1; pp. 3–4, Section 3.1
evidence.detail: The paper motivates separating expensive future generation from control and defines observation/language-conditioned action chunks, a 16-step 20 Hz action horizon and approximately three-second foresight.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 4–5, Section 3.2, Three-role training window and Two-pass causal visual encoding
evidence.detail: Training separates observations, a noised full-horizon future and a clean intermediate lookahead. Two causal-VAE passes encode the generative and policy streams independently within a shared video-DiT architecture.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.2, Non-interfering 3-class attention mask
evidence.detail: Observation queries read observations; future queries read observations/future tokens; lookahead queries read observations/lookahead tokens. The prose claims identical observation/future representations to standard co-training.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.3, Equations (1)–(2)
evidence.detail: The shared backbone and action head optimize summed video/action flow losses. Video conditioning contains observation latents and language; the inverse-dynamics action objective additionally consumes observation/lookahead features and offset.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 5–6, Section 3.3, Staleness-robust horizon randomization and Multi-layer visual extraction
evidence.detail: The lookahead offset is sampled uniformly over (0,H_f], embedded sinusoidally and paired with 0.1 lookahead dropout. Multi-layer features come from layers 5, 12, 19 and 26.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 3.4
evidence.detail: The proposed schedule generates a lookahead once per approximately three-second horizon, retains it without RGB decoding and reuses it across roughly four 0.8-second chunks with a decaying offset.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 6–7, Section 4.1, datasets, baselines and training details
evidence.detail: RoboCasa uses 24 tasks, 50 demonstrations per task and 1,200 held-out evaluation episodes. LIBERO uses four ten-task suites and 2,000 episodes. External baselines are publication results; GlanceWAM trains for 10,000/15,000 steps from SkyReels-V2-DF using demonstrations.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Table 1, GlanceWAM and Cosmos Policy rows; p. 7, Section 4.2
evidence.detail: The reported RoboCasa success rates are 72.2% for GlanceWAM and 67.1% for Cosmos Policy, each using 50 demonstrations per task. Section 4.2 disambiguates the compressed final table row.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Table 2, Avg column; p. 7, Section 4.2
evidence.detail: Reported LIBERO averages are 99.0% for GlanceWAM, 98.5% for Cosmos Policy and 97.6% for Fast-WAM.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Table 3, all internal rows; p. 8, Section 4.3 and footnote 1
evidence.detail: Success is 64.4% without lookaheads, 71.5% with single-layer conditioning, 61.6% after zeroing that checkpoint and 72.2% with multi-layer conditioning. Training-step comparisons are explicitly not compute-matched.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Table 4, Euler steps and SR rows; p. 10, Section 4.5
evidence.detail: Paired evaluations of the single-layer checkpoint use 1,200 episodes per point. Success at 1, 2, 5, 10 and 30 steps is 71.2, 71.7, 71.4, 71.5 and 69.8 percent.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Section 4.3, How far ahead should the prediction target be?
evidence.detail: The prose reports lookahead-horizon results of 66.3% at 1.4 seconds, 71.6% at 3.0 seconds and 71.1% at 3.8 seconds.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 13–14, Appendix B, Protocol and Deployment inference path
evidence.detail: The cached-lookahead LIBERO path uses eight actions and four action-flow steps on an A100 40 GB. It measures 47.95 ms with 0.39 ms standard deviation. Optimizations include blocks 1–27, compilation and caching. Listed phase times are 8.1, 28.1, 0.6 and 12.1 ms; serving overhead is described as approximately 1–2 ms.

evidence.location: PDF p. 14, Appendix B, Lookahead refresh and Same-hardware baseline comparison
evidence.detail: An unoptimized generate-then-act refresh costs 478.6 ms at ten steps and approximately 145 ms at one step. The stated refresh cadence is 3–4 seconds. Fast-WAM's compiled 91.5 ms measurement uses a 32-action chunk.

evidence.location: PDF p. 15, Appendix C, Why does a self-generated lookahead help?
evidence.detail: The authors propose additional amortized test-time computation and a destination/action training scaffold as compatible explanations, explicitly stating that the evidence does not separate them.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 15–16, Appendix D.1, definitions and paired staleness experiments
evidence.detail: Training covers hold aging but not source staleness. Every-chunk proposals adopted one 0.8-second chunk later achieve 70.8% versus 71.3% synchronously, p=0.72. Naive delays of 0.8/1.6/3.2 seconds achieve 68.8/60.5/49.9%, with a 62.7% zeroed reference.

evidence.location: PDF p. 17, Appendix E
evidence.detail: The appendix specifies latent compression and patch sizes, four H200 GPUs, bf16, batch size 64, AdamW parameters, separate backbone/head learning rates, cosine scheduling, warmup, gradient clipping, dropout and EMA.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section 2, Test-time imagination and efficiency; p. 6, Section 3.3, Multi-layer visual extraction
evidence.detail: These passages state an 8.4% foresight gain and a 1.3% multi-layer improvement, respectively, differing from the corresponding increments calculable from Table 3.

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, Abstract, final sentence
evidence.detail: The authors state that code is available at their linked GlanceWAM GitHub repository; the supplied reading contains no repository inspection or independent reproduction.
